Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Box 11.6, Principle of Ambiguity and Goals.
:::

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.5.

- Goal-setting remains uncertain even when the process is organized. Revisit goals as new information becomes available.
- Proverb: aim higher than you expect to achieve: real execution tends to fall short regardless
- **Three substantive bullets, honest picture of reality**:
  - Early design phase = genuine ambiguity; architect's job to resolve it into small/complete/consistent/humanly-solvable goals (callback to 11.4's five criteria as the target state)
  - No single person controls the whole upstream process: expect uncoordinated, incomplete, conflicting inputs; not an unusual failure, the normal state
  - Context/needs keep evolving (latent needs, Kano drift): needs an ongoing *process* to reexamine/update goals, not a one-time kickoff activity

**Discussion:** Can numerical goals eliminate all ambiguity?

**Suggested answer:** No. Units, conditions, populations, methods, and interpretation still matter. A precise number can measure the wrong outcome or conceal disagreement about the system's purpose.

:::

## Consistency and Attainability {.smaller}

- **Logical consistency:** targets using the same metric must not contradict each other
- **System consistency:** goals such as low mass, long range, and high acceleration interact. The shape and severity of those tradeoffs may require an analytical model
- Some metrics add directly, such as component mass. Others emerge from the interaction of the architecture's elements
- **Attainability:** check technology, development schedule, resources, and risk together. Derivative products offer more evidence than entirely new designs
- If the goal set cannot be attained, revise its scope or add resources. Assess whether the model is reliable enough to support that choice

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.5.

- **Deeper on two of the five criteria**: subtle, not simple checkboxes
- **Consistency**: many real goals conflict (e.g. range vs. battery weight). Not enough to know a tradeoff exists: need its *shape*: shallow, steep, or non-monotonic? Often can't assess by inspection: needs an analytical model (low- or high-fidelity), and you must separately trust the model's accuracy
- **Attainability**: reachable given technology, schedule, resources, risk. Much easier for derivative products than clean-slate designs (higher tech/schedule risk)
- Two levers when goals aren't attainable: **reduce scope**, or **add resources**: no third option
- Course's V&V coverage is deliberately shallow (covered in dedicated SE texts): Part 4 returns to attainability with explicit cost models

**Suggested answer:** Model the coupled goals over the candidate design space and test whether any feasible architecture meets their thresholds simultaneously. For range and battery mass, capacity can increase stored energy while also increasing vehicle mass and energy demand, so the relationship need not be linear. Examine the tradeoff curve, assumptions, and uncertainty before relaxing a goal. An infeasible result can indicate conflicting goals, an overly narrow concept set, or an inaccurate model; it does not automatically identify which goal should be discarded.

:::

## Verification and Validation {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](assets/chapter11/fig11_17_verification_loop.jpg){width=100% height=410px fig-align="center"}
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
- **Validation loop:** delivered function meets stakeholder needs
- **Verification loop:** delivered values meet goal metrics and targets
- Five checks: **representative, complete, humanly solvable, consistent, attainable**
- Models help test the goal set as the concept and form develop
:::
:::

::: {.side-caption}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 11.17.
:::

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.5.

- **Compact visual summary tying together all five criteria**: where each gets checked as a project proceeds from goal-setting to delivered system
- **Outer path**: upstream influences → goals (metrics + targets) → concept → form → intended function → functional deployment → delivered function
- **Validation loop**: "is the goal representative?": compares delivered function against the original upstream influences. Checks whether we built something addressing real stakeholder needs, not just a self-consistent spec
- **Verification loop**: the other four criteria (attainable, complete, consistent, solvable): compares delivered goals against concept/form/intended function, using a model where needed
- Maps onto classic V&V: verification = "did we build the system right?" (per its own goals); validation = "did we build the right system?" (per real upstream needs). Can pass verification and still fail validation if goals were never truly representative: why Representative sits apart, checked by its own loop

**Suggested answer:** Verification asks whether the system meets its specified goals; validation asks whether those goals and the delivered outcome address the original stakeholder needs in context. A vehicle can meet its specified test-cycle consumption and still disappoint a user whose real route and load were omitted. Passing a self-consistent specification therefore does not establish that the right system was built. Trace goals back to needs and test representative use as well as specification compliance.

:::

## Section 11.5 Summary {.smaller}

- Prioritize goals as **critical, important, or desirable** to guide resource decisions
- Record **rigidity separately** from importance, including constraints associated with the chosen market
- Specify **metrics, target values, and applicable conditions** so success can be assessed
- Use logical checks and models to assess consistency and attainability
- Verify performance against goals and validate that the delivered function meets stakeholder needs. Update the goals when the evidence changes

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.5.

- **Closes 11.5 before chapter wrap-up**: students should be comfortable with:
  - Critical/important/desirable tiers and resource allocation
  - Every goal needs a metric, target value, and rigidity (constraining vs. unconstrained), not just prose
  - Consistency/attainability checks often need analytical modeling, not just inspection: tied together in the validation/verification-loop diagram
- All four Fig. 11.1 steps now complete: next slide pulls the whole chapter together before the Nagano case study

**Discussion:** What should the team do if no candidate meets all goals?

**Suggested answer:** Check the model and search coverage, then examine whether goals conflict or the concept set is too narrow. Revisit priorities with stakeholders rather than silently dropping a requirement.

:::

## 11.6 Chapter Summary {.smaller}

- Complex systems face real challenges managing stakeholders: many of them, often with unclear relative priority, sometimes providing only non-monetary inputs, and often delivering value indirectly
- Value delivery is an **exchange**: your outputs meet their needs, and their outputs meet yours
- Stakeholders should be **prioritized by the inputs they provide to the project**: directly or through indirect value loops
- Needs are translated into **goals** via the System Problem Statement and the To-By-Using framework, then checked against five criteria and prioritized as critical/important/desirable

::: {.callout-tip title="Reference"}
Crawley, E., Cameron, B., & Selva, D. (2016). *System Architecture: Strategy and Product Development for Complex Systems*. Pearson. Chapter 11.
:::

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.5.

- **Full-chapter recap**: walk back through Fig. 11.1 one more time
- **Three opening challenges**: many stakeholders; unclear relative priority (especially non-monetary inputs like political support vs. revenue); value often delivered *indirectly* through intermediaries
- **Process built in order**:
  - Identify stakeholders/beneficiaries via exchange-based value (definitional anchor + completeness check)
  - Characterize needs (Kano as key tool)
  - Treat stakeholders as a system: stakeholder map, indirect transactions, value loops, network-based prioritization
  - Translate needs into goals (enterprise-defined, not beneficiary-owned) via SPS + To-By-Using, checked against five criteria, prioritized critical/important/desirable
- Why this matters: Chapter 12 takes this prioritized goal set for the Hybrid Car as the starting point for generating/evaluating concept alternatives: none of that is possible without this groundwork

**Discussion:** What distinguishes a useful goal set from a long specification?

**Suggested answer:** It represents important needs, is complete enough for the decision, and is consistent, attainable, and humanly solvable. Length alone provides none of these guarantees.

:::

# 11.7 Nagano Winter Olympics: Stakeholders in IT Architecture

## Scope of the Nagano IT System {.smaller}

*By Dr. Victor Tang, Director of IT Client Relations for IBM's 1998 Olympic Winter Games*

- IBM was contractually obligated to build, operate, and maintain the **entire IT system** for the Games: computing and delivering competitors' results, accrediting athletes and staff, recording drug-testing results, and more
- 25 million lines of software; 10 mainframes, 5,000 PCs, 1,500 printers, 160 servers, 2,000 routers: serving ~150,000 athletes, officials, and volunteers
- A genuine **system-of-systems**: each constituent system has a different stakeholder, with distinct priorities, interests, and biases

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.7.

- **Unusual provenance**: written directly by Dr. Victor Tang, IBM's actual Director of IT Client Relations for the 1998 Games: first-hand practitioner account, not a retrospective
- **Scale and stakes**: IBM, one of 11 top sponsors (~\$60-80M sponsorship), contractually obligated to build/operate/maintain the *entire* IT system: results computation/delivery, athlete records, accreditation, drug-testing results, more
- Numbers: **25M lines of software**, 10 mainframes, 5,000 PCs, 1,500 printers, 160 servers, 2,000 routers, serving ~150,000 athletes/officials/volunteers
- **Genuine system-of-systems** (Ch. 2 emergence): each constituent system has its own distinct stakeholder (IOC, media, games admin, sports federations, Nagano Organizing Committee...) with different priorities/interests/biases: not one clean customer, exactly the hard multi-stakeholder situation this chapter built tools for

**Discussion:** Why is an Olympic IT service more than a collection of computers?

**Suggested answer:** Its value depends on timely, correct information and coordinated event operations. People, procedures, interfaces, and service continuity are part of the system delivering that outcome.

:::

## Nagano IT Systems and Stakeholders {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](assets/chapter11/fig11_18_nagano_it_system.jpg){width=100% height=430px fig-align="center"}
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
- **Core systems:** Athlete Qualification, Games Management, Results, and INFO98
- **Stakeholders:** organizers, sports federations, media, volunteers, medical and transport services
- Athlete and results data cross subsystem boundaries
- Each constituent system serves different priorities. The architecture must support the Games as a whole
:::
:::

::: {.side-caption}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 11.18.
:::

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.7.

- **Concrete visualization of the system-of-systems scale**: four core systems (Athlete Qualification, Games Management, Results, INFO98) connected by athlete/results/bio data flows
- Surrounding client-facing layer: press, scoreboards, local print, TV graphics/commentator info, medical, accreditation, volunteers, transportation, accommodation, data collection, email/info retrieval
- Echoes the chapter's stakeholder-map exercises: same logic, real historical high-stakes system, mostly data flows instead of money/goods
- **Discussion prompt**: how would you identify the primary beneficiary and prioritize among all these stakeholders? No single obviously-dominant beneficiary like the Hybrid Car's driver/owner: hard, and the rest of the case study shows IBM navigating exactly this

**Suggested answer:** Begin with the event's mission and identify the beneficiaries of each service, rather than forcing one person to dominate the entire network. Athletes and officials need correct competition administration and results; broadcasters, press, and spectators depend on timely trustworthy information; organizers need reliable operations. Prioritize needs by consequence of failure, time criticality, binding commitments, and downstream dependence, then agree on service levels. Correct results may be an essential prerequisite for many other services even when those services have more visible users. The diagram identifies dependencies but cannot supply stakeholder weights by itself.

:::

## Rethinking IBM's Strategy {.smaller}

- At Atlanta in 1996, immature technology and poor execution damaged confidence in IBM
- For Nagano, IBM framed the mission as an **IT service that helps people run the Games**
- This changed the system boundary: reliable operations and stakeholder processes became part of the architectural concern
- **X-teams** connected domain experts across organizational boundaries. IBM invited stakeholders into development and embedded its engineers in stakeholders' processes
- Participants gained a better understanding of reciprocal dependencies and became credible advocates for the work

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.7.

- The Atlanta Games exposed problems with products and technology that were not ready, damaging confidence before Nagano.
- Chapter's core theme (needs vs. goals, getting the problem statement right) plays out at enormous real stakes
- **IBM's strategic shift**: from product-technology-centric to products/technology as *the means* to deliver a *service*. Publicly stated: "IT as a service...helping those running the Games, run the Games...enhancing the Olympic experience"
- **Connect to Ch. 2's system boundary**: IBM literally *moved the boundary*: not "IT products IBM builds" with organizers as an external customer, but redrew the boundary to include the organizers' success itself
- Exactly the difference between solution-specific "By/Using" (specific IBM tech) and solution-neutral "To" (successfully running the Games): the To-By-Using discussion almost exactly

**Discussion:** How did a service-oriented framing change the IBM case's problem?

**Suggested answer:** It put successful Games operations at the center and treated technology as an enabling means. That changes priorities from showcasing products to supporting users' operational outcomes.

:::

## Responsibilities Without X-Teams {.smaller}

![](assets/chapter11/fig11_19_without_xteams.png){width=95% height=310px fig-align="center"}

- IBM owns requirements, specifications, software, and documentation
- Sports, news, and NAOC mainly review test work. Their operational knowledge enters late

::: {.side-caption}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 11.19.
:::

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.7.

- Read columns left to right: IBM, Xerox, Sports, News, NAOC, IOC. Blank cells mean no role shown in this figure.
- Xerox does some test-case writing and test execution. Sports, News, NAOC, and IOC mainly review tests, then concur on performance and training.
- IBM only concurs on training; Xerox does and concurs. Do not infer that IBM created training in this baseline.
:::

## Responsibilities With X-Teams {.smaller}

![](assets/chapter11/fig11_19_with_xteams.png){width=95% height=310px fig-align="center"}

- Xerox joins requirements and specifications work
- Sports, news, and NAOC help create and run tests and contribute to training
- IBM retains software responsibility while stakeholders participate more broadly

::: {.side-caption}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 11.19.
:::

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.7.

- IBM still does the requirements, specifications, software, and documentation work. Xerox now also does and reviews requirements and specifications.
- Sports, News, and NAOC move from reviewing test cases to doing and reviewing them. IOC continues to review test cases.
- Sports, News, and NAOC also move from concurring on training to doing and concurring. IBM still only concurs; Xerox still does and concurs. Performance concurrence does not change.

**Discussion:** Which change would most directly reveal a misunderstood sports rule before the Games?

**Suggested answer:** Having sports-domain participants help write and execute test cases, rather than only review IBM's finished cases.
:::

## What the X-Team Comparison Shows {.smaller}

- Requirements and specifications gain early input from Xerox and broader review from the operating stakeholders
- Sports, news, and NAOC representatives help write and run tests and participate in training
- IBM retains responsibility for software and documentation. Wider participation complements its technical work
- Performance concurrence remains the same. The changed responsibilities concentrate on requirements, tests, and training
- The organizational arrangement helps reveal **needs and reciprocal dependencies** that document review alone can miss

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.7.

The precise role matrix matters because “co-development” does not mean everyone jointly did every task. X-teams brought domain knowledge into decisions and tests where it could prevent misunderstandings. Compare this to Box 11.1's distinction among consultation, participation, and decision rights.
:::

## Rebuilding Trust Through the ICPG Process {.smaller}

IBM's four “Must Do” goals were:

- Meet all technical and management requirements
- Avoid surprises during the Games
- Provide 24/7 operations
- Provide highly secure and usable systems

**International Competitions Prior to the Games (ICPGs)** provided practice events using the rules and IT systems.

IBM convened federations, IOC representatives, and stakeholders to review documented errors. They agreed to treat resolving those errors and shortcomings as satisfying the requirements, making the work tractable through **management by exception**.

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.7.

- **Four "IBM Must Do" goals** from the Atlanta debrief: meet all technical/management requirements, no surprises during the Games, 24/7 operations, highly secure/usable systems: reads exactly like Section 11.5's critical-goals category
- **Clever practical move**: tackling "meet all technical and management requirements": the full documented requirement set (Seiko timing, Xerox printing/distribution, accreditation/security, volunteer training, more) was "voluminous," daunting to fully satisfy
- **ICPGs (International Competitions Prior to the Games)**: real practice events (often existing World Cup competitions) testing new/modified Olympic rules and IT systems under live conditions first
- Formal plenary convocation on ICPG performance: federations/IOC came with documented errors/shortcomings from practice events. After negotiation: solving all *documented* errors became the agreed interpretation of "all requirements"
- Turned an impossibly vague, unverifiable goal into something tractable: anchoring "complete" to a concrete, finite list. A clever practical instance of making a goal "humanly solvable" under organizational pressure

**Discussion:** What kind of evidence can rebuild trust after a service failure?

**Suggested answer:** Shared, testable commitments and demonstrated progress against operational needs. A new promise or feature list is weaker than evidence that dependencies and responsibilities are understood.

:::

## Architecture as a Utility {.smaller}

- IBM treated IT as a **secure, usable utility** that continuously supplies data and information
- Networked servers provided the equivalent of a utility's plant and distribution grid. Applications generated the structured data used by clients
- Existing Athlete Qualification, Games Management, Results, and INFO98 systems formed the core. The design had to reuse, modify, or protect legacy systems
- The Results System decomposed into venue subsystems, connecting Seiko timing inputs to scoreboards and information services
- **Redundancy** duplicated key components so a failed component could be replaced by its counterpart while operations continued

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.7.

- **Open with the Louis Sullivan quote** (skyscraper's inventor): connect to Ch. 7's concept/form material: architecture is a mapping from function-space to form-space, and meaningful architecture needs workable *concepts* embodying an abstract idea into a real, functioning artifact
- Book calls this **embodiment of an idea**: the most creative, challenging part of architecting; brilliant architectures need brilliant embodiments, not just correct requirements
- **IBM's concept, worth spelling out in full**: re-conceptualized the system as a *utility* (highly secure, plug-and-play),
  - networked servers = power plant/distribution grid (24/7 availability, satisfies one of the four "Must Do" goals)
  - applications = generators
  - structured data = the utility's actual output, serving stakeholders/public as clients
- Honest detail: this concept was initially received with **reserve and skepticism**: sound architectural reframing doesn't automatically earn buy-in; trust still had to be built (ICPG process + X-teams doing exactly that in parallel)
- **Results System**: most important subsystem (processes actual competition performance data): stepwise decomposition (per competition venue) + **reliability through redundancy**: key components duplicated throughout (timing interfaces, PCs, LANs, WANs, databases, mainframe/medium servers)
- No single point of failure could take down the whole system during the live Games

**Discussion:** What follows from treating the IT architecture as a utility?

**Suggested answer:** Users expect dependable service rather than needing to understand its internal products. Reliability, support, interfaces, and operational ownership become central architectural concerns.

:::

- **Results** connects competition entries and timing to media, scoreboards, and commentator information
- **Accreditation** supports access and athlete/staff services

- Data and function flows integrate the legacy systems into a coherent service for the Games

Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 11.20.

Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.7.

- The utility metaphor becomes a concrete service architecture: results are collected and distributed to scoreboards, commentators, broadcasters, and information services.
- Accreditation supports security and access-related services; INFO98 distributes information through management, email, and terminals.
- Ask which interfaces need timely and trustworthy results. The figure represents data and service flows, not ownership of every connected organization.

## Results System Redundancy {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](assets/chapter11/fig11_21_nagano_redundancy.png){width=100% height=410px fig-align="center"}
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Follow **capture, ranking, database update, and distribution**
- **A/B paths** duplicate timing, event control, databases, and output interfaces
- The pattern supports the critical continuity goal
- Test interfaces and failover. Duplicating hardware alone cannot establish continuity
:::
:::

::: {.side-caption}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), Fig. 11.21.
:::

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.7.

- Follow the primary and backup Seiko timing inputs through A/B timing interfaces, event controllers, database servers, ORTO output, scoreboard control, and CIS controllers.
- Duplication helps a working path continue if one component fails, but the drawing alone does not establish independent failure modes or guarantee availability. Test failover and shared infrastructure.
- This architectural pattern is tied to the critical goals of 24/7 operations and no surprises during the Games.

**Discussion:** What needs testing beyond having two servers?

**Suggested answer:** Failover detection and switching, data consistency, common network/power dependencies, and end-to-end output to scoreboards and broadcasters.
:::

## Data Flow and Reliability Serve the Stakeholders {.smaller}

- Correct results must reach the scoreboard, broadcasters, commentators, and information services when they need them
- The Results System's A/B paths support the critical availability goal, while shared interfaces still require integration and failover testing
- IBM's service framing ties these technical choices to event operations and user trust

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.7.

Use Figures 11.20 and 11.21 together. Figure 11.20 identifies who depends on the information; Figure 11.21 shows one way to protect its production and distribution. Ask students to trace a result from Seiko's timing input to a scoreboard and to name where a backup path must take over.
:::

## Lessons from the Nagano IT Project {.smaller}

- **Architecture expresses business policy.** IBM's service mission gave stakeholders a common basis for judging technical decisions
- **The architect remains accountable for system integrity.** Implementation responsibilities must be delegated across a large organization
- X-teams brought stakeholder expertise into requirements, testing, and training
- Practice competitions converted broad expectations into an agreed body of issues to resolve
- Data flows, legacy integration, and redundancy supported the operational goals. The IOC's favorable assessment after the Games supported the service approach

::: {.notes}
Source: Crawley, Cameron & Selva (2016), §11.7.

- **Two headline lessons IBM itself drew: connect each back to the chapter's themes**, the purpose of closing on this case study
- **Lesson 1**: paraphrase of Clemenceau (war too important to be left to generals): IT architecture too important to be left entirely to technical experts, since IT is a technical *expression* of business policy. Must be positioned within that context to be meaningful to decision-makers, stakeholders, users: restates this chapter's core argument: architecture grounded in real needs/goals, not technical elegance alone
- **Lesson 2**: architect is always **accountable** for overall system integrity, but not personally **responsible** for implementation: implementation must be delegated. Especially critical for large-scale social/technical systems: no one person could implement it alone, but someone must hold the integrated whole together and answer for whether it works
- **Close on the resolution**: IBM entered Nagano with zero IOC confidence after Atlanta. Afterward, IOC Director General Francois Carrad (not known for handing out compliments) said: "Technology at the Winter Games in Nagano has been outstanding"
- Validates not just engineering execution but the *strategic reframing*: IT as a service, moved system boundary, X-teams co-development, ICPG tractability: everything this case study, and the chapter, built toward

**Discussion:** Which lesson from Nagano transfers to a small campus project?

**Suggested answer:** Define the user's successful activity before selecting technology, involve the people who must operate the service, and test the complete workflow rather than only individual components.

:::
